cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights in the UK
cards.back: The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR): drafted in 1950, ratified by the UK in 1951. Protects fundamental rights: right to life (Article 2), prohibition of torture (Article 3), right to liberty (Article 5), right to a fair trial (Article 6), right to privacy (Article 8), freedom of expression (Article 10), freedom of assembly (Article 11), and right to marry (Article 12).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights in the UK
cards.back: The Human Rights Act 1998: incorporated ECHR rights into UK law. UK courts can now hear human rights cases without going to Strasbourg. Courts can declare legislation 'incompatible' with the ECHR (but cannot strike it down - Parliament decides). Public authorities (including the government, police, councils) must act compatibly with ECHR rights.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights in the UK
cards.back: Key rights explained: Right to life (Article 2): the state must not take life arbitrarily and must investigate deaths. Right to a fair trial (Article 6): independent tribunal, presumption of innocence, right to legal representation. Freedom of expression (Article 10): can say what you think BUT restrictions apply (hate speech, defamation, national security).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights in the UK
cards.back: Balancing rights: rights are not absolute - they can be limited where necessary and proportionate. Freedom of expression vs protection from hate speech. Right to privacy vs freedom of the press (Max Mosley case). Right to liberty vs national security (terrorism legislation). Courts balance rights on a case-by-case basis.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights in the UK
cards.back: Debates: should the UK leave the ECHR? (Some Conservatives argue it limits sovereignty; others argue it protects fundamental rights.) Should the Human Rights Act be replaced with a British Bill of Rights? (Proposed but controversial - could weaken protections.) Rights come with responsibilities: the right to free speech comes with the responsibility not to use it to incite hatred.

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — human rights in the uk?
cards.back: 1. For Human Rights in the UK questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link Human Rights in the UK to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
Evaluate whether the Human Rights Act 1998 effectively protects citizens' rights in the UK.

cards.front: Understanding Human Rights in the UK in British Context
cards.back: Human Rights in the UK is a core topic in GCSE Citizenship Studies that requires understanding of how the UK political and legal systems work, and how citizens can participate effectively. The specification requires you to know how British democracy functions, understand your rights and responsibilities as a citizen, and be able to take informed and responsible action on citizenship issues.

cards.front: Human Rights in the UK and UK Democratic Processes
cards.back: The UK is a parliamentary democracy where citizens exercise power through elected representatives. Understanding human rights in the uk requires knowledge of how democratic processes work: general elections (first past the post), devolved elections (additional member system for Scotland and Wales), local elections, and referendums. cards.front: Rights, Responsibilities and Human Rights in the UK
cards.back: UK citizens have both rights and responsibilities. Key rights include: the right to vote, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, the right to a fair trial, and the right to privacy. These rights are protected by the Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
